focus_area_title: Shared Governance to Reduce Overtime/Improve Turnover
content_text_body:
Managing staffing and scheduling in a healthcare environment is challenging. Ensuring that the right staff and the right numbers of staff are in place to ensure safe patient care while also balancing the workload of healthcare professionals is an ongoing and complex problem. A shared governance model may offer some solutions to these problems.

### Why is it important?

Several studies demonstrate the importance of proper staffing levels on patient safety. Two studies released in 2011 found that higher nursing levels improved patient outcomes, often saving lives. Proper staffing also improves employee engagement and reduces the possibility of burnout amongst healthcare professionals making for an environment better suited for overall safety. Finally, when organizations begin to improve the efficiency of their staffing, they save significant money that would've been spent on agency nursing or overtime pay.

A shared governance framework involves staff at all levels throughout the organization having autonomy and flexibility with their schedules.  According to Dr. Karlene Kerfoot, a long-time healthcare professional and nurse staffing expert, these models can improve overall employee engagement and reduce turnover.  A shared governance structure can take the form of a nursing committee or any staff-led organization that takes into account the concerns of frontline healthcare workers. **Below are some suggestions to implement a shared governance model:**
 
- **Reach out to those impacted by staffing decisions**  
Before making any changes to your staffing procedures, reach out to those frontline workers impacted by these decisions to ensure their voices are heard and considered in any decision-making moving forward. This relationship building can be very helpful in the long-term in improving engagement.

- **Seek to Understand how Changes Will Impact Workflow**  
Andrea Erickson, MSN, RN, CNML, director of inpatient critical care services at Lowell General Hospital, credited Shared Governance in helping her roll out a new Acuity-Based staffing system at her hospital. Along with other key stakeholders, 6-10 staff RN's helped make up a large task force of individuals who met regularly to determine how best to implement this new staffing methodology across the system. Erickson discussed the importance of understanding how these changes would affect work areas, resources, and staff educational needs - information they primarily received from those on the front-lines of care. She also emphasized the necessity of preserving nursing's voice in the process. "At the end of the day, we want an acuity-tool system that fulfills requirements of the law, but we don't want to lose nursing judgment along the way," she said. 

- **Ensure a Partnership**  
According to Porter-O'Grady and Hinshaw, two researchers who've done significant work on shared governance, they state that this partnership links healthcare providers and patients along all points in the system. They believe that partnership is essential to building relationships, involves all staff members in decisions and processes, implies that each member has a key role in fulfilling the mission and purpose of the organization, and is critical to the healthcare system's effectiveness.

- **Ensure Equity**  
Porter-O'Grady and Hinshaw also believe this is the best method of integrating staff roles and relationships into structures and processes to achieve positive patient outcomes. Although equity does not mean equality in terms of knowledge, authority, or responsibility, it does mean that each team member is essential to providing safe care. 

- **Ensure Accountability**  
The authors describe this as a willingness to invest in decision-making and express ownership in those decisions. Accountability is the core of shared governance.
